lesson.title: Three Letters at a Time: Codons Meet Their Anticodons
lesson.summary: An mRNA is read three nucleotides at a time as codons, and each codon is recognized through complementary base pairing with a matching three-nucleotide anticodon carried on a transfer RNA.
lesson.body:
An mRNA molecule, built from the same four ribonucleotides covered under nucleotides and RNA structure, adenine, uracil, guanine, and cytosine, is not read one base at a time. It is read in groups of three, called codons, and the reason comes down to simple arithmetic. There are only twenty standard amino acids to specify, but only four possible bases at each position. Reading one base at a time gives just four possible codes, nowhere near enough. Reading two bases at a time gives sixteen combinations, still short. Reading three bases at a time gives sixty-four possible combinations, more than enough to cover all twenty amino acids with room to spare, which is exactly the system life actually uses.

A codon on its own does nothing; it has to be recognized by something that can physically deliver the correct amino acid. That something is a transfer RNA, or tRNA, and the part of the tRNA that does the recognizing is a three-nucleotide sequence called the anticodon, which pairs with the mRNA codon using the same base pairing rules covered earlier, adenine with uracil and guanine with cytosine, but arranged in an antiparallel orientation, meaning the two three-base sequences line up running in opposite directions. Take the codon 5'-UUU-3', which specifies the amino acid phenylalanine. For a tRNA to deliver phenylalanine at that codon, its anticodon has to pair against UUU in antiparallel fashion, matching a U with an A at each of the three positions; reading that anticodon in the standard 5' to 3' direction gives 5'-AAA-3'. Lined up against the codon, it reads 3'-AAA-5' pairing with 5'-UUU-3', with A pairing to U all the way across.

Pairing at the first two codon positions tends to be strict, but pairing at the third position is often looser, a flexibility known as wobble that lets a single tRNA anticodon recognize more than one codon. That detail will matter again once we look at why the genetic code has more codons than amino acids. For now, the key idea to carry forward is this: codon-anticodon pairing is the physical event that converts the nucleotide language of mRNA into the amino acid language of protein, and it is the step that every stage of translation ultimately depends on.
